evidence.title: Learning How to Love You
evidence.text: "Learning How to Love You" is a song by English musician George Harrison, released in 1976 as the closing track of his debut album on his Dark Horse record label, "Thirty Three & 1/3".

evidence.title: Learning How to Love You
evidence.text: Harrison wrote the song for Herb Alpert, sometime singer and co-head of A&M Records, which at the time was the worldwide distributor for Dark Horse.

evidence.title: Learning How to Love You
evidence.text: Although the relationship with A&M soured due to Harrison's failure to deliver "Thirty Three & 1/3" on schedule, resulting in litigation and a new distribution deal with Warner Bros.

evidence.title: Learning How to Love You
evidence.text: Records, Harrison still dedicated the song to Alpert in the album's liner notes.

evidence.title: Thirty Three & 1/3
evidence.text: Thirty Three & ⅓ (stylised as Thirty Three & 1/ on the album cover) is the seventh studio album by English musician George Harrison, released in November 1976.

evidence.title: Thirty Three & 1/3
evidence.text: It was Harrison's first album release on his Dark Horse record label, the worldwide distribution for which changed from A&M Records to Warner Bros. as a result of his late delivery of the album's master tapes.

evidence.title: Thirty Three & 1/3
evidence.text: Among other misfortunes affecting its creation, Harrison suffered hepatitis midway through recording, and the copyright infringement suit regarding his 1970–71 hit song "My Sweet Lord" was decided in favour of the plaintiff, Bright Tunes Music.

evidence.title: Thirty Three & 1/3
evidence.text: The album contains the hit singles "This Song" – Harrison's satire on that court case and the notion of plagiarism in pop music – and "Crackerbox Palace".

evidence.title: Thirty Three & 1/3
evidence.text: Despite the problems associated with the album, many music critics recognised "Thirty Three & ⅓" as a return to form for Harrison after his poorly received work during 1974–75, and considered it his strongest collection of songs since 1970's acclaimed "All Things Must Pass".

evidence.title: Teardrops (George Harrison song)
evidence.text: "Teardrops" is a single by George Harrison, released on 20 July 1981 in the United States and 31 July in the UK.

evidence.title: Teardrops (George Harrison song)
evidence.text: It was the second single from the album "Somewhere in England" and reached number 51 on the US "Billboard" Top Tracks chart and number 102 on the "Billboard" Bubbling Under the Hot 100 chart.

evidence.title: Teardrops (George Harrison song)
evidence.text: In Japan, it was released on 25 September.

evidence.title: Soft Touch
evidence.text: "Soft Touch" is a song by English musician George Harrison from his 1979 album "George Harrison".

evidence.title: Soft Touch
evidence.text: It was also issued as the B-side of the album's lead single, "Blow Away", apart from in North America, where it was the B-side of the second single, "Love Comes to Everyone".

evidence.title: Soft Touch
evidence.text: Harrison wrote the song while in the Virgin Islands with his future wife, Olivia Arias, shortly before recording his 1976 album "Thirty Three & 1/3".

evidence.title: Soft Touch
evidence.text: The song is a love song in which Harrison also conveys his wonder at the idyllic island setting.

evidence.title: What Is Life
evidence.text: "What Is Life" is a song by the English musician George Harrison, released on his 1970 triple album "All Things Must Pass".

evidence.title: What Is Life
evidence.text: In many countries, it was issued as the second single from the album, in February 1971, becoming a top-ten hit in the United States, Canada and elsewhere, and topping singles charts in Australia and Switzerland.

evidence.title: What Is Life
evidence.text: In the United Kingdom, "What Is Life" appeared as the B-side to "My Sweet Lord", which was the best-selling single there of 1971.

evidence.title: What Is Life
evidence.text: Harrison's backing musicians on the song include Eric Clapton and the entire Delaney & Bonnie Friends band, with whom he had toured during the final months of the Beatles.

evidence.title: What Is Life
evidence.text: Harrison co-produced the recording with Phil Spector, whose Wall of Sound production also employed a prominent string arrangement by John Barham and multiple acoustic rhythm guitars, played by Harrison's fellow Apple Records signings Badfinger.

evidence.title: Love Comes to Everyone
evidence.text: "Love Comes to Everyone" is a song by English musician George Harrison that was released as the opening track of his 1979 album "George Harrison".

evidence.title: Love Comes to Everyone
evidence.text: It was also issued as the second single off the album.

evidence.title: Love Comes to Everyone
evidence.text: The recording contains musical contributions from Steve Winwood and Eric Clapton.

evidence.title: Dark Horse Records
evidence.text: Dark Horse Records is a record label founded by former Beatle George Harrison in 1974.

evidence.title: Dark Horse Records
evidence.text: The label's formation coincided with the winding down of the Beatles' Apple Records and allowed Harrison to continue supporting other artists' projects while maintaining his solo career.

evidence.title: Dark Horse Records
evidence.text: The initial signings were Indian musician Ravi Shankar and Splinter, the last of whom provided the label with its only significant commercial success until Harrison signed with Dark Horse in 1976.

evidence.title: Dark Horse Records
evidence.text: The label was distributed internationally by A&M Records for the first two years of its operation.

evidence.title: Dark Horse Records
evidence.text: Following a highly publicised split with A&M, Harrison and Dark Horse formed a long-term partnership with Warner Bros.

evidence.title: Dark Horse Records
evidence.text: Records that lasted until the expiration of his contract in 1994.

evidence.title: Somewhere in England
evidence.text: Somewhere in England is the ninth studio album by George Harrison, released in 1981.

evidence.title: Somewhere in England
evidence.text: The album was recorded as Harrison was becoming increasingly frustrated with the music industry.

evidence.title: Somewhere in England
evidence.text: The album's making was a long one, during which conflicts with Warner Bros.

evidence.title: Somewhere in England
evidence.text: Records arose.

evidence.title: Somewhere in England
evidence.text: "Somewhere in England" was the first Harrison album to be released after the death of his former Beatles bandmate John Lennon; the lyrics of its first single, "All Those Years Ago", pay tribute to Lennon.

evidence.title: Best of Dark Horse 1976–1989
evidence.text: Best of Dark Horse 1976–1989 is a compilation album by English musician George Harrison, released in October 1989.

evidence.title: Best of Dark Horse 1976–1989
evidence.text: His second compilation, after the Capitol/EMI collection "The Best of George Harrison" (1976), it contains songs from Harrison's releases on his Dark Horse record label between 1976 and 1987.

evidence.title: Best of Dark Horse 1976–1989
evidence.text: The album also includes a 1989 single, "Cheer Down", which was Harrison's contribution to the soundtrack of the film "Lethal Weapon 2", and two tracks recorded specifically for the collection: "Poor Little Girl" and "Cockamamie Business".

evidence.title: Best of Dark Horse 1976–1989
evidence.text: Despite the popularity of Harrison's work over this period – both as a solo artist with his "Cloud Nine" album (1987), and as a member of the Traveling Wilburys – the compilation failed to achieve commercial success.

evidence.title: When We Was Fab
evidence.text: "When We Was Fab" is a song by English musician George Harrison, which he released on his 1987 album "Cloud Nine".

evidence.title: When We Was Fab
evidence.text: It was also issued as the second single from the album, in January 1988.

evidence.title: When We Was Fab
evidence.text: The lyrics serve as a nostalgic reflection by Harrison on the days of Beatlemania during the 1960s, when the Beatles were first referred to as "the Fab Four".

evidence.title: When We Was Fab
evidence.text: Harrison co-wrote the song with Jeff Lynne, who also co-produced the track.

evidence.title: When We Was Fab
evidence.text: The recording references the psychedelic sound that the Beatles had helped popularise in 1967, through its use of sitar, cello, and backwards-relayed effects.

evidence.title: When We Was Fab
evidence.text: Harrison's former Beatles bandmate Ringo Starr is among the other musicians on the track.

evidence.title: When We Was Fab
evidence.text: The single was accompanied by an innovative music video, directed by the partnership of Kevin Godley and Lol Creme.

evidence.title: When We Was Fab
evidence.text: One of Harrison's most popular songs, "When We Was Fab" has appeared on the compilations "Best of Dark Horse 1976–1989" (1989) and "" (2009).
